M18.1:
Visit on February 23, approximately 25 minutes, at the High Desert Neurology office in Boise. This was my third interaction with this prescriber since October 2025 and the first to run the full scheduled slot.

The agenda was set by the physician rather than by me. The interest here is post-stroke seizures — called an overlooked population in every registry reviewed so far. I was told that these referals arrive from the stroke service and from two outlying hospitals, and that the practice has no standard pathway for them once the acute period has passed. A request was made for any published work on that group; I confirmed only that I would ask Medical Information what exists in the public literature, and I made no claims and discussed no product in connection with that population.

The remainder of the conversation stayed at the level of the general ASM landscape, meaning how many agents the practice keeps in routine use and how often the formulary list is reviewed. No comparative or efficacy statements were made by either party.

Follow-ups from my side: (1) submit the literature request on seizures following stroke, (2) confirm which XCOPRI resources are cleared for field use at label level, (3) ask the coordinator for a thirty-minute slot rather than the usual fifteen. Next contact expected the second week of April.

M19.1:
Visit 15 June, late morning, abt 15 min in the back office. Second try, first appt got bumped in May.

All of it was teaching. Practice takes two neurology residents a block from the affiliated program, plus one PA student this summer. Says the resident weeks are useful but notes take twice as long when every one of them gets precepted before it closes.

Journal club is regional, rotates between three sites, next one lands here in September. Wants the residents picking the papers insted of the faculty. Asked whether that changes who is allowed to sit in. I said I would check what is permitted for an MSL to observe and would confirm nothing until I hear back.

Also mentioned fellowship applications are due in the fall and two residents want letters, which falls the same week as the September session. Front desk is short one person, so the September logistics land on the same coordinator.

No clinical questions. No product discussion at all, none raised by me either. No materials requested, nothing owed on my side.

Next: e-mail the observer answer once I have it. Aim for a proper appt in Aug, keep it short.

M20.1:
Visit on June 22, 2026, 14:10 to 14:45 local, at the Richmond office. Fourth contact with this practice in 2026; the previous visit was March 4.

Discussion centered on the older segment of the panel, which the physician put at roughly 40 percent of the focal-onset caseload and rising each year since 2023. Asked for a concise interaction table for elderly patients on five or more concomitant medications. The format wanted was specified: one page, printable, organized by drug class rather than by product, and current enough to leave with a covering colleague.

Context given for the request. Of the patients over 65 seen in May, about half arrived on six or more medications, and each new consideration triggers a seperate pharmacy review that adds five to seven days. Two of those reviews last month came back with questions the office could not close without calling the pharmacist twice.

No efficacy discussion took place and no dosing was discussed. I confirmed that anything I bring will be cenobamate label-level material and that I cannot advise on individual patients.

Follow-ups: request the cleared interaction reference from Medical Information, confirm by July 6 whether a one-page version already exists, and book the next visit for the week of August 10.

M21.1:
Caught the attending between clinic and EEG reads, abt 12 min, resident workroom.

Whole thing was paperwork. Prior auth volume is the complaint. Epilepsy service runs everything thru one coordinator now and the queue sits 2-3 days behind on a good week. Three payers, three portals, same info in three formats.

Appeals are the worse part per this prescriber. Denials come back by fax, staff re-key them, then a peer to peer gets booked at 4:30 when nobody is free. Estimated a handfull of hours a week across the service, no exact count kept.

Said the pattern is the same whichever agent is being requested, so nothing product specific to log from this visit. I raised no product topics and none were raised at me.

Also noted the dept is asking for a dedicated auth FTE in the next budget cycle, and that two f/u clinics got collapsed into one afternoon to free the coordinator up.

No materials requested. Nothing owed except scheduling.

Next: try for a real appt in Sept, prob after the 10th. Book thru the coordinator, not e-mail.

M22.1:
I met with the attending on the afternoon of July 8 at the Mesa office. The slot was only twenty minutes, but the conversation was unusually substantive and the physician did most of the talking.

The visit opened with an unprompted account of one patient. Described a drug-resistant adult who went from weekly seizures to rare breakthroughs after titration. The patient had cycled through several regimens over a number of years before being started on XCOPRI last winter, and what seemed to strike this prescriber most was that the change has held through the spring rather than fading after the first weeks. I recorded the account as a single individual experience, noted that no denominator was offered, and was careful neither to generalize from it nor to draw any comparison with other agents.

We then spent a few minutes on practical matters, namely the follow-up interval used for patients in that situation and how the office captures seizure counts between visits so that a change is not missed.

I was asked politely whether any published long-term data on refractory adults could be shared, and I said I would route the question to Medical Information rather than answer from memory. Nothing else was requested of me. The visit closed on the July heat and a flight out of Phoenix that had been delayed twice.

M23.1:
Visit 27 April, abt 20 min, borrowed office on the third floor.

Topic was volume. Referrals up over last quarter, mostly two regional hospitals and the ED. New pt slots gone thru mid August. F/u interval stretched to five or six months for stable patients, which nobody likes.

Cause per the attending is coverage, not demand. One epileptologist out on sabbatical til fall, and the surgical conference eats a half day a week. Same referrals sit longer.

Video EEG is the real bottleneck. Monitoring beds run full, admissions get pushed a week or two, discharge summary backlog follows behind that.

Numbers get reported up quarterly and the pressure is to shorten the new pt wait, so f/u clinic absorbs it. Expects it to even out once the sabbatical ends. Fellows carry more of the f/u load meanwhile.

No clinical discussion. No product topics from either side, no materials requested, nothing to action. Logged for context only.

Next: check in end of June, ten min max. Coordinater prefers Tues or Thurs.

M24.1:
Visit on May 18, approximately 30 minutes, at the Madison center. Second interaction with this attending in 2026, and the tone was more direct than in February.

The discussion opened with the adolescent handoff into the adult service, described as the least satisfying part of the week. The comment was that cenobamate is probably safe for adolescents too, and that stopping the label at 18 seems arbitrary. I have recorded the remark as stated rather than paraphrasing it, and I want to be explicit that it is the opinion of the physician and not something I introduced, endorsed, or took further. My only response was to confirm that the approved indication is limited to adults and that I am not able to discuss use outside it. No material relating to patients under 18 was provided, offered, or promised.

The remainder of the visit was administrative: prior authorization paperwork across the center, now handled by a single coordinator, and one payer that asks for the same information in two formats. No product specifics arose in that part of the conversation.

Follow-ups from my side: (1) flag this interaction to my manager and to compliance on the day of the visit, per procedure, (2) send only the cleared adult indication summary and nothing beyond it, (3) reconfirm at the next visit that no request for unapproved information is left outstanding.

M25.1:
Visit on July 15, 2026, 09:30 to 09:55 local, at the Cedar Ridge office in Springfield. Third contact this year; the previous visit was April 21.

The entire conversation concerned the building work. The medical office building shares a lot with the hospital campus, and the garage rebuild that began in March is scheduled to run through February 2027. Two of the three entrances are closed, and the practice moved its check-in desk on May 4 to the corridor beside the elevators.

Practical consequences described: the staff lot is now a nine to ten minute walk, the shuttle runs twice an hour rather than every fifteen minutes, and roughly six patients a day arrive late or at the wrong door because the exterior signage still directs to the old lobby. The office added a reminder call two days before each appointment, which the front desk estimates costs an extra hour of staff time daily.

No clinical or product topics were raised during the visit, and I did not introduce any. No materials were requested and nothing is owed on my side.

Follow-ups: use the north entrance and allow twenty extra minutes on the next visit, and book the following meeting for the week of October 12.
